Tents from a well-known outdoor retailer seem to be overpriced to me, and for backpacking, they appear pretty heavy for what you get. It's basically over-engineered and charges boutique pricing. For backpacking, though, you have a *ton* of options around that retailer's price point (it's no longer a minor brand name; you're paying for the label at this point). Stoves like Jetboils are fine if you're wanting to boil water quickly and don't mind the weight, but they lose speed and efficiency if you're camping anywhere with more than a breeze. They aren't efficient in the wind at all. For me, at least, they are quite heavy. The titanium option wasn't bad, but I don't think they make that anymore.

For roughly the same price, I can get a micro rocket or a similar model and something like a titanium pot and save half a pound or more on my cooking kit.

I could also go with a cone kit and an alcohol stove solution and go quiet and a little slower (about 7-10 minutes to boil water). If I upgraded to titanium, I'd be carrying less weight than the other two options. Plus, once you buy your stand-alone pot, it can be moved between systems. The Jetboil is pretty much only usable with its own systems. You're locked in.

For sleeping bags, check out a company that specializes in lightweight gear. They actually sell closed footbox quilts. I really like them since they combine the lightness of a mummy bag and the comfort of... well... a blanket. They're also economical compared to the competition.

Making your own taco seasoning is very easy, and if you want to share with your dogs, you can leave out the onion powder.

Seasons roughly 1lb of meat

* 1 tablespoon chili powder
* 1/4 teaspoon garlic powder
* 1/4 teaspoon onion powder
* 1/4 teaspoon crushed red pepper flakes
* 1/4 teaspoon dried oregano
* 1/2 teaspoon paprika
* 1 1/2 teaspoons ground cumin
* 1 teaspoon sea salt
* 1 teaspoon black pepper

I use this without thickeners and just let it reduce until it's fairly saucy. Works well. I also tend to omit the red pepper flakes or at least reduce them if I am not in the mood for heat. If you want a thickener to create a more traditional taco seasoning sauce, you could probably add some corn starch or maybe some xanthan gum (though not much, a little goes a long way and too much creates a slimy consistency). Adjust salt to taste, and consider cutting down the teaspoon of black pepper. It makes things quite peppery.

Well first note that it is designed to use trekking poles. I can't remember if the site has standalone poles, but those will obviously add to the weight.

Setup- Stake the 4 corners out. The tent has a bathtub with carbon fiber stays in it which are great for keeping the bathtub floor intact. The top corners loop over your stakes (this is a little trickier if you can't stake things down. You're going to need rocks or extra line or some creativity to do it. I talked to someone who pitched the tent on camping platforms using cordage and rocks). Then you unzip the tent, and there's a little plastic/carbon fiber stay in there that's bent (I think it's rigid plastic) at just the right angle that velcros in. Take your hiking pole, stick the tip in the plastic tube, and shove the round handle down into the middle of the tent. Repeat on the other side. I usually crawl in, hold it up, and pitch that way. Adjust height for tautness.

You're basically done at that point. The awning rolls up or pulls down and can be propped open with a stick. Dropping it into storm mode is basically as easy as pulling the stick out and maybe having a stake or a rock or branch or something to tie down on. Pretty easy.

It takes a little getting used to and you absolutely want to pitch it a few times in your backyard before getting out on the trail. Make sure you use a groundsheet (you can order one from the website if you don't want to deal with it) because the ground bathtub is silnylon and pretty thin. It's just safer to pitch on top of a groundsheet.

In better weather you can roll back the awnings and get some real airflow through the tent, which is another reason I like it.

When you boot up a personal computer, it goes through a Power On Self Test before loading the master boot record into memory and interpreting that to start loading the operating system. It's entirely possible to say, pull a city during an outbreak, add 3 cubes, discard, shuffle the discard, then place it back on the infection deck, and then during the infect phase *draw that city again*.

Edit: Okay so here's the epidemic rules:  
1. Increase the infection draw rate token one space.

2. Infect: Draw a city from the bottom of the deck and put 3 cubes on it. Discard this city into the discard pile.

3. Intensify: shuffle the infection discard pile and place it on the top of the infection deck.

Proceed with turn as normal (usually either drawing one more card or proceeding to the infect stage).

Basically, after the first epidemic, the game is going to concern itself with mostly the cities that you've already seen develop diseases, with the occasional epidemic throwing a new city into the mix for fun. Depending on how the epidemics were loaded into the deck at the beginning of the game, you may see more cities as you get higher infection rates and have more than your average turns between epidemics. But the cities that you pull at the start of the game until your first epidemic are always going to be your worst "problem" cities. They'll always keep showing up.
To be specific, don't shuffle the discard directly into the infection deck, shuffle the discards and then place on top of the infection deck.

The next time you go through an infection phase, a major city is now on top of the deck and may get a cube added to it. Then it gets discarded and stays out of play until the next epidemic. Then it goes back into play and is at risk again.
But you don't during the infect phase at the end of the turn. Epidemics add *new* locations to your problem. Infections (at least in the beginning) just make existing problems worse.

A calorie is the amount of energy it takes to raise 1 gram of water by 1 degree Celsius. Its equivalent is around 4.2 joules. 

A joule is the amount of work or energy exerted by 1 newton of force to move the point of exertion one meter in the direction of the force.

A joule is considered the SI unit of energy.

And a newton is the force required to accelerate 1 kilogram by 1 meter per second squared.

Since they are such small measurements, we deal in kilojoules and kilocalories, though because of common practice, we refer to kilocalories simply as calories, as there is often resistance to metric terminology.

If you're in the United States, you can get a rotisserie chicken for around 5 dollars from a large retail store or warehouse club. When I don't want to cook, I opt for the rotisserie option. I also have a microwave steamer tray and will buy some green beans, broccoli, cauliflower, or a frozen vegetable mix to steam, then add a drizzle of sesame oil for extra flavor. It takes less than 5 minutes to steam veggies in the microwave, and the rotisserie chicken can provide meals for a day or two. Once it's finished, if you're feeling adventurous, you can use a pressure cooker or slow cooker to make some chicken stock from the leftovers, which feels quite productive.

One of my comfort foods is tomato soup. Get a large can of whole peeled tomatoes, dump it into a pot. Add several tablespoons of butter, half of a roughly chopped onion, and about 1.5 cups of chicken stock, vegetable stock, or water. Season with a little salt and pepper, then let it simmer for 45 minutes. Blend with an immersion blender or pour into a blender and mix in batches. If you want a bisque, add a few tablespoons of cream. Adjust seasoning with salt, pepper, and maybe a bit of sugar if the tomatoes taste too canned. It’s a very low-effort, incredibly tasty tomato soup. Pair it with a sandwich or a side salad for a complete meal.

A final serious suggestion: consider sous vide cooking. It can be a bit pricey to start, but you essentially fill a large pot with water, insert your immersion cooker, set the temperature, and place your protein (and even vegetables) in a ziplock or vacuum-sealed bag, removing most of the air. Let it sit in the hot water for an hour or two. Timing is flexible with sous vide, so if you need extra time to prepare, it will be ready when you are. You usually just need to finish the protein with a quick sear in a hot pan for about 60 seconds on each side. I also prepare a semi-complicated sous vide sweet potato that involves cooking for an hour at a lower temperature to enhance sweetness, then increasing the temperature to soften the sweet potatoes. Asparagus cooks in about 10 minutes, and there are many other vegetables you can prepare this way. It's a fascinating cooking method.

At a certain point, you care based on traffic shaping, firewalls, access control lists, etc. But at a rudimentary level, you really don't care what kind of data is being sent.

As for why one device accepts data from another, at a networking level, the frames and packets are announcing that they are destined for the receiving device. The network interface card verifies that the frames are indeed for it, and the operating system verifies that the IP address is indeed its own. Depending on whether the traffic is TCP or UDP, there may be some bi-directional communication between the devices to facilitate data transfer, but again, that's a higher level than what you're probably dealing with at this point.

The OSI model breaks down how data is sent from one device to another. You need to learn it and understand it. I've been doing this for nearly 20 years now, and I still go back to the OSI model to conceptualize what is going on when troubleshooting.

I never really get what people mean by saying they want to send data to another network.

Data means all the parts of a frame or packet that aren't used for navigation. So for a frame, anything that is not the destination MAC address, source MAC address, Ethernet type, or checksum is the data. At the switch level, it never looks at the "data" payload. For a packet, it's similar, but the construction of a packet has different fields. But again, at the level that you're at, we don't even look at the data payload. Something further up the OSI model will look at that.

Understanding encapsulation and decapsulation is important.

That's a long process but let's see if I can abbreviate it.

Email is actually a kind of complicated multi-step process (assuming you're acting as your own email host) where you have to do an MX record lookup before you even send the email. So we're going to be abstract.

Layer 6 & 7 are the Operating System infrastructure and applications. Let's say you're playing a popular sandbox game with its server. You need to send information to the server on what you're doing. So the game and the operating system are essentially layers 6 & 7 and kind of beyond our scope. The application creates a protocol data unit of "game instructions" and hands that off to the networking protocol stack in the operating system. The operating system then packages those up into UDP datagrams (TCP has bi-directional communication and we aren't going there yet, UDP is just best effort but generally faster. Layers 6 & 7 have to detect data loss and re-request data, whereas TCP can detect lost data and request a retransmission). It then hands off the datagrams, which include a destination, to the IP stack, which encapsulates the UDP datagram into an IP packet. This packet has source and destination network info and uses logical IP addresses. It will chunk up the UDP datagram into multiple packets because the TCP packets are smaller than the UDP datagrams. It will then pass the packets on to the layer 2 network interface card (NIC) processor, which will break the packets into smaller frames and encapsulate them with destination and source addresses and a checksum. These addresses are MAC addresses—hardware addresses on the NIC. The NIC then takes these frames and passes them off to the Layer 1 portion of the NIC, which generates electrical impulses across the wire.

Let's say you're plugged into the router directly. The router picks up the electrical signals at its ethernet port and reassembles them into frames. It then looks at the frame destination and says "Yup! that's for me!" otherwise it drops the packet and ignores it. But this is a good packet, so it strips off the frame header and tail and decapsulates it, leaving just the data. It then passes that up to the TCP level of the router, which assembles the data frame payloads into a packet. It then looks at the packet's destination address and determines what port to send the packet out. It routes the packet out to that port, re-packages it into frames to hop to the next router's interface/MAC (assuming we're using ethernet all the way), and then the port breaks down the data into electrical impulses and sends the data as bits and bytes. The next router does the same thing, reassembling the frame, then making sure it should be the right destination before stripping the frame delivery information and passing the data back up to the router to assemble into layer 3 packets. The router says "Hey! This packet is on my network!" and routes it out the local network interface, following the same process. It then re-encapsulates everything down to frames and then forwards the bits and bytes out.

Computer B gets these bits, and then reassembles them. It looks at the frame and says "Yup that's me!" and strips the frame information off and passes the data up to layer 3. The IP layer 3 reassembles the packets and looks at the destination IP and says "yup! That's me!" and pulls off all the IP transit information and hands it up to layer 4/5 UDP, which takes the packets and assembles them into UDP datagrams and says "Cool story bro, this looks like a good datagram for a port that I have open" and strips the UDP information off and then hands it off to the operating system, which says "Oh this is meant for the game! Here you go game" which finally analyzes that you've clicked your mouse button to swing your axe. Now the game needs to tell Computer A "message received" or "send that again please" and the whole process repeats in reverse and so on ad nauseum.

Congrats. You've just sent data from computer A to computer B, and they're on different networks. If they're on the same network, there are no routers, just a switch or two, and the switches operate at Layer 2 and never look at IPs. Just MAC addresses (There are exceptions but let's not go there). The only devices in that scenario that will look at IPs will be the end computers to make sure the packets are meant for them.

I've left a ton of information, details, exceptions, etc... out but that's the rough basics that I can type out while I should be working.

Glad to help. Once you understand how stuff gets passed between OSI layers, things start making sense. So now when someone talks about a Layer 3 device, you know in the real world it's basically talking about IP addresses, and that usually means routers (or multi-layer switches, which, as I said, is a complication for another day).

Dealing with depression is tough. I tend to binge eat as a way to cope when I'm feeling down and stressed, so I understand what you're going through.

When the urge to indulge in unhealthy food strikes, take a deep breath, close your eyes for a moment, and do a physical self-assessment from your head to your toes to really tune into what you're feeling physically. Then, check in with your thoughts and emotions. There’s often an underlying emotion and a quiet narrative in your mind that triggers the binge. You need to acknowledge it, even if you don’t confront it directly.

If possible, practice delayed gratification. When you crave junk food, tell yourself, "Okay, but I have to wait 15 minutes," and then engage in something that requires your full attention, perhaps after drinking a big glass of water or having a coffee. Ideally, choose an activity that demands focus. Even engaging in a debate on a discussion forum can help. The goal is to distract yourself from the immediate craving. Chances are, after 15 minutes, the urge will have diminished. If it hasn’t, go ahead and enjoy the treat. You made a deal with yourself and honored it, so it’s important to be honest. Just remember, each time you give in, you’ll need to wait an additional 5 minutes next time. If you resist the urge, the waiting time decreases by 5 minutes. Over time, you’ll find a balance where you can manage the craving more effectively.

The best hypothesis I've seen for "the woosh" is that when you burn fat from your fat cells, they temporarily replace the lost energy with water, expecting to get filled back up again. At some point your body finally gets the message that the fat recharge is just not going to happen any time soon, so your fat cells expel the water, you pee/breathe/sweat it out, and... woosh! the weight drops. 

As I said, I don't know if this is really what happens, but the woosh seems to be real, and it's as good of an explanation as I've encountered. You may be in that interim, and how long it lasts is different for everyone.
